text.p: BRUSSELS, Oct 14, Reuter - The European Union's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), created in 1979, provides a zone of relative stability in the European currency markets.

As of Monday, when the Finnish markka was brought into the system, the ERM counts 11 of the bloc's 15 national currencies. Italy's lira, Britain's pound, Sweden's crown and Greece's drachma remain outside.
All 15 currencies, however, are part of the European Monetary System (EMS), which means they are included in the calculation of the European currency unit (Ecu).

The ERM is designed to keep currencies trading in a range around a central rate. Since August 1993, most currencies have been allowed to fluctuate by as much as 15 percent above or below the fixed central cross rate against each other.
The German mark and the Dutch guilder trade informally within 2.25 percent bands, the original range for all the ERM currencies until the bands were burst open in a currency crisis in August 1993.
When a currency hits the permitted floor or ceiling value against another ERM unit, the two central banks concerned must intervene to hold it within its band by buying or selling as required.
This does not, of course, apply to the four currencies outside the grid, although they are bound by unspecific treaty language to keep their curencies stable.
Italy's lira is widely expected to be the next currency in the ERM after it was expelled out in September 1992 together with the pound following intense market speculation.
